A SQL studio that asks the schema, not the whole database
Engineers were pasting schemas into chatbots and watching the prompt explode. We built a workbench that prunes the right tables, then writes dialect-aware SQL.
NL2SQL that survives a real schema

Naive NL2SQL dumps the whole schema into the model. On a real database that is a 413 — token limit, not a clever answer. Desktop GUIs don’t help either: they run SQL, they don’t know which twelve tables the question actually needs. Teams behind a VPN often have a Prisma file and no live connection at all.

We treated the schema as a graph, not a blob. Every dialect — Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, plus CSV via DuckDB in the browser — normalises to one contract. Before the model sees anything, a local embedder ranks tables, walks one foreign-key hop, then clamps to a token budget. Offline import (Prisma, DDL, JSON) is a first-class mode, not a demo.

A Vue 3 studio (Monaco, results grid, ERD, copilot) talking to a Fastify API. Connections are per-user. Read-only guards sit on the same path as the AI. Groq writes, explains, and fixes SQL. Embeddings stay local so we don’t pay a second vendor for vectors. Writes don’t sneak through because someone phrased the prompt aggressively.

The studio runs against live databases: connect, prune, generate, explain, copy out. Large hub-and-spoke schemas no longer blow the prompt. You can import a shape with no live DB, get SQL, and take it back to the real engine. Public demo is still coming. The product already does the job.
From job requisition to shortlist without leaving the desk
Hiring lived in inboxes, calendars, and a spreadsheet of open roles. We built one recruiting desk — requisitions, sourcing, matching, and interviews — so the pipeline has a place to live.
One desk from JD to next interview

A requisition opened in one tool. CVs arrived in another. Matching was a recruiter’s memory. Interviews were a calendar invite with no link back to the role. Hiring managers saw a dump; recruiters saw a queue. VIP referrals — the ones that must not get lost — landed in the same inbox as everything else.
They didn’t need another ATS brochure. They needed the week of hiring to happen in one place.

We started from the requisition, not the candidate list. Every later step has to point at a JD: sourcing, match scores, pools, interview slots. Recruiters and hiring managers get different shells of the same product — same data, different jobs. Referrals get their own qualify path, because a stakeholder intro is not a job-board apply.

A Vue 3 recruiting workspace: create and progress job requisitions, run sourcing against the open role, score candidates against the JD with a matching pass the recruiter can actually read, keep silver-medalists in CRM pools, and put interviews on a shared calendar. Live updates so two people don’t edit the same stage in the dark. Enterprise SSO so the desk sits inside the company, not beside it.
The matching UI is not a magic percentage in a vacuum. It sits on the advert — the headings the role already uses — so a score means “this CV against this job,” not “this CV against the universe.”

The pipeline is visible. A recruiter can open a requisition and see who is sourced, who matched, who is waiting on a slot, without exporting to Excel. Hiring managers review a shortlist, not a folder. Referrals get qualified instead of buried. The product is private — we talk about the desk, not screenshots of other people’s candidates.
Daily earnings and expenses, not a notebook by the till
Barbershops were tracking jobs, cash, and worker splits on paper. We built a multi-tenant desk for today’s work — and the pay math that actually matches the chair.

The chair was busy. The books were not. Jobs lived in a notebook, expenses in a chat, and “what does Ahmed take home?” was a monthly argument. Commission, salary, and an optional shop levy all meant different things in different shops. A Super Admin still needed plans and quotas without becoming IT for every salon.

We designed for today first: clock in, log the haircut, log the expense, see earnings and net before close. Pay rules are shop settings, not a spreadsheet the owner redoes at night. Workers see their jobs and their share. Owners see the shop. Super Admin sees plans, not every rupee.

A Next.js app on Postgres: shops, workers, services, jobs, expenses, attendance. Commission splits (and levy-then-split) are calculated in one place so a Rs 300 haircut doesn’t get three different answers. Monthly salary shops keep job cash in the till and show salary on the statement. Auth is JWT over REST so a Capacitor Android/iOS shell can reuse the same API. Trial shops hit a daily action quota so the plan means something.

The owner opens Today and sees the day — not a reconstruction. Workers clock in and log jobs without touching the owner’s ledger. Plans and quotas keep the multi-tenant layer honest. The shop still cuts hair. The software finally counts it the same way twice.
Airport sedan bookings that don’t die in a quote email
A limo and shuttle desk was quoting by hand, then retyping the same trip into a booking. We built quote and reservation as one flow — cars, drivers, add-ons, and pay.
Quote to confirmed trip in one path

Airport sedan, shuttle, and limo work is simple until it isn’t: surge windows, add-ons, affiliates, a driver who has to be assigned, a customer who started with “just a quote.” The public site and the back office were two stories. Quotes aged in inboxes. Confirmed trips hid in another list.

We made “Get a quote” and “Make a reservation” the same product with different intent. Cars, drivers, customers, discount codes, and surges share one admin. The customer never re-enters a trip the desk already priced.

A Nuxt 3 front with a Node API: reservation create/update/detail, driver assignment, add-ons, affiliates, and payment through PayPal and Braintree. Roles and permissions for who can touch which list. Static pages and config for the marketing skin without forking the app. Socket updates when a trip changes status so the desk isn’t refreshing to see if the driver accepted.

A quote is a reservation that hasn’t been confirmed yet — not a parallel spreadsheet. The same cars and drivers the customer sees are the ones the desk assigns. Payments and refunds sit on the trip, not in a separate merchant tab someone might forget.
A hospitality desk with three ways to get paid
Pick-up and drop work needed a real reservation system — customers, call-center staff, and admins — plus Stripe, PayPal, and Braintree on the same trip.

The operation already had cars and drivers. What it didn’t have was one record of the trip. Customers booked one way, the phone desk another, finance reconciled cards in three merchant dashboards. Status lived in someone’s head. A refund meant hunting a transaction ID.

We modelled the trip as the object everyone shares: customer, assigned drivers, add-ons, payment type, status. Super admin, call-center users, and customers see different doors into the same booking. Gateways are adapters on the reservation, not three products.

A Vue 2 + Express app on MySQL: reservations from draft to paid, driver assignment with optional email, add-ons, affiliates, discount codes, surges. Stripe, PayPal, and Braintree webhooks land on the same reservation so finance isn’t guessing which processor owns the fare. Live status over Socket.io. Roles so a call-center user can’t wander into super-admin config.

A trip has one number, one payment, one driver list. Refunds point at the reservation, not a spreadsheet of merchant exports. The hospitality desk can take the booking on the site or on the phone and still be looking at the same record.
The phone desk that books the same inventory as the website
Agents were taking airport transfers on the phone and typing them into a tool that didn’t match the public booking. We built the operator console on the same cars, drivers, and fares.
Phone bookings on the live fleet

The website could book a sedan. The phone could not — not without a side channel. Agents worked from a different list of cars, guessed surges, and assigned drivers the public site didn’t know about. By the afternoon, two versions of “what’s on the road” existed.

We didn’t build a CRM with a notes field. We put the agent on the same reservation object the customer uses: search, filter, draft, assign, collect payment type. The console is dense on purpose — a headset shift is not a marketing page.

A Vue 2 operator app: reservation queue with status, payment type, customer and transaction IDs, assigned drivers. Side filters instead of a pretty dashboard. CRUD for cars, add-ons, discount codes, affiliates, and surges so the person on the call isn’t waiting on an admin in another building. Live updates when a trip changes while they’re still on the line.
A booking taken at the desk is a real reservation on the fleet — same cars, same drivers, same fare rules. The agent isn’t the integration layer. The inventory is.
A freight site that answers two different questions

A nationwide truck dispatching company connects two different audiences — truckers looking for loads, brokers looking for trucks. We built a site that gives each one their own path from the first click.
Two audiences, two paths, one site

A dispatch company sits between two audiences who want opposite things from the same homepage. A trucker wants to know: will you keep me loaded? A broker wants to know: can I trust your trucks? One generic "our services" page makes both of them read past copy meant for someone else before they find their answer.

We split the message at the door instead of burying it in a submenu. "I Need Truckers" and "I Need Loads" branch immediately, each with the proof that audience actually checks — insured loads, no long-term contracts, and a vetted carrier network read differently depending on which side of the load you're on. We didn't try to make one page satisfy both.

An Astro site built for speed over spectacle: dedicated pages for Dispatch Services, Carrier Sign-Up, About, and Contact, dispatcher profiles that put a face on "someone will actually answer," and carrier and broker testimonials sorted by who they're meant to convince. Click-to-call and email sit up front as the primary CTA, not a support ticket — this business runs on live conversation, not a queue.
A visitor lands, sees their own path within seconds, and gets to a real person fast. No default homepage trying to be everything to everyone.
Inventory, products, and orders in one portal, not three spreadsheets

A multi-location food chain tracked stock, products, and orders across spreadsheets and manual logs. We built one real-time portal so staff see the whole operation without stitching it together by hand.
One dashboard, real-time stock and orders

A food chain running multiple locations had inventory in one place, the product catalog in another, and orders tracked by whoever picked up the phone or the clipboard. Nobody had one clear picture of what was in stock, what was actually for sale, or what was still owed to a customer — just a set of logs that had to be cross-checked by hand.

We built around the three things staff touch every shift: what's in stock, what's for sale, and what's been ordered. One dashboard, not three systems loosely taped together. Role-based access so day-to-day staff see what their shift needs, without wading through settings meant for management.

A centralized portal covering inventory management (stock levels, usage, shortages across locations), product management (the full catalog in one place), and order management (create, track, and fulfill from a single dashboard) — on an architecture built to add locations without a rebuild.

Staff get a real-time view of operations instead of relying on spreadsheets or manual logs. Fewer manual errors, less time reconciling numbers that should already match, and a clearer picture of the business at a glance.
From paper tickets to one digital record, photos included
A U.S. collision repair shop ran every job — intake to completion — on paper and scattered phone photos. We built one system for the repair order and the image record that goes with it.
One digital record per vehicle, photos included

Collision repair runs on paperwork and photos — before shots, damage notes, progress photos, the final result — and most of it never made it into one place. The repair order lived on paper. The photos lived on someone's phone. Months later, "what happened to this car" meant asking around the shop.

We treated the repair order and its photo record as one object, not two separate workflows. Every stage of a job — intake, in-progress, completion — carries its own images, searchable against the order that owns them. Built around how a U.S. collision shop actually moves a car through the floor, not a generic ticketing system repurposed for auto repair.

A digitized workflow that replaces paper and scattered folders: repair orders tracked from intake through completion, photos captured and stored directly against each order, and a centralized job history so every vehicle's repairs — and the evidence of them — live in one searchable place.

Shop owners and staff get a single source of truth for every car that comes through the door — better accountability, a real record without the paper, and less time hunting for who has the photos from a given job.
